description: How a stage is executed: inline in the current session, as a subagent, or as an agent team. Left to arbitrary model choice this becomes expensive and inconsistent, so each stage declares it.

inline.meaning: The current session does the work.
use_when: the operator wants to watch it happen

subagent.meaning: A focused worker with its own context that reports its result back to the caller.
use_when: the task is focused and bounded
only the result matters, not the working
the caller will act on the result
subagent.token_cost: moderate: the result is summarised back into the caller's context
subagent.notes: Default for reviewers, analyses and single-artifact production.

team.meaning: Independent Claude Code instances with their own contexts, direct messaging and a shared task list.
use_when: workstreams are genuinely independent and can run in parallel
specialists need to challenge each other rather than report separately
do_not_use_when: the work touches the same files AND the workers share one checkout, because parallel edits overwrite. This is now a fork, not a stop: see 'isolation'. Give the workers separate worktrees and a declared merge step, or run them sequentially.
team.token_cost: high and roughly linear in teammate count: each teammate is a full instance
team.size: 3 to 5 teammates. Beyond that, coordination cost grows faster than throughput.

isolation.description: Which working copy a parallel worker edits. 'Do not edit the same file' used to be the whole rule, and it is not enough: sometimes one file genuinely must be edited twice, and a rule that can only say no turns into a smaller plan or a silent overwrite. Claude Code has first-class git worktree isolation, so the answer to a real collision is a separate working copy plus a merge step that someone owns.

shared-checkout.meaning: Every worker edits the session's working directory. This is what a worker gets when nothing is said.
use_when: the workers own disjoint paths and none of them runs a build, a test suite or a formatter
the workers are read-only, which covers every reviewer and every investigation
shared-checkout.risk: Two writers to one file: last write wins, and the loser's work disappears without an error.

worktree.meaning: The worker runs in its own git worktree under .claude/worktrees/ of this repository, on its own branch. Its edits are invisible to the main checkout and to every other worker until they are merged.
use_when: two workers must change the same file, or the same generated artifact
a worker runs a build, a test suite, a formatter or a code generator, all of which write shared output
a worker installs or upgrades dependencies, which rewrites a lockfile
a long worker must not leave the main checkout half-edited if it is abandoned
the work is exploratory and may be thrown away
do_not_use_when: the worker is read-only: a reviewer in a worktree reviews a copy, and the isolation buys nothing but a checkout
the worker must see uncommitted work in progress in the main checkout, which by default it will not

how.spawned_worker: Agent(subagent_type=..., isolation: "worktree"). Mutually exclusive with cwd. The worker is told it is in a worktree and that its changes do not affect anyone else.
how.agent_definition: isolation: worktree in the agent's frontmatter, for a role that should always be isolated. 'worktree' is the only value valid for a plugin-shipped agent.
how.current_session: EnterWorktree to move this session into a new worktree (or into an existing one by path), ExitWorktree with action 'keep' or 'remove' to leave it. Use only when a human asked for a worktree, or project instructions require one.

worktree.returns: When the worker changed nothing, the worktree is removed automatically. When it changed something, the result carries worktreePath and worktreeBranch. Those two values are what makes the merge a step rather than an archaeology exercise.
worktree.cost: A second working copy per worker on disk, and a checkout per spawn. In a large repository set worktree.sparsePaths and worktree.symlinkDirectories in .claude/settings.json before deciding it is too slow.

integration.rule: An isolated worker's output is not in the repository until someone merges it. A stage that spawns isolated workers declares the integration step and its owner in the same place it declares the workers. An undeclared merge is how parallel work becomes a branch nobody owns.
integration.owner: The lead that spawned the workers. Never a worker: a worker cannot see the others' branches.
steps: Collect worktreePath and worktreeBranch from every worker result. A worker that returned neither changed nothing, and has nothing to merge.
Merge the branches into the integration branch one at a time, in a stated order, so a conflict names one worker.
Resolve conflicts as the lead, in the integration branch. Do not send a conflict back to a worker whose worktree no longer reflects the merged state.
Run the build and the full test suite once, after the last merge. Every worker's green run was against its own copy and proves nothing about the union.
Only then is the stage's output produced. Review and approval apply to the merged result, not to the individual branches.
on_conflict: A conflict between two workers is evidence the split was wrong, not just a merge to resolve. Record it: the same split will be proposed again next time.
A conflict on a coupled surface named in policies/coupling-policy.json is a policy failure, not a merge problem. The surface has one owner; the merge is not the place to decide it.

what_the_plugin_can_enforce: No workflow stage declares an isolation mode yet, so nothing validates one. When a stage does, validation should require it to declare the integration step and its owner in the same place. Stated here so the gap is a known omission rather than an assumed guarantee.
A PreToolUse hook on Agent sees the spawn's tool_input, including isolation, so it can refuse a spawn. It cannot add isolation to one.

What is enforced today is coherence: tests/test_execution_isolation.py fails if this policy, docs/execution.md and skills/team-patterns/SKILL.md stop naming the same mechanisms, or if this policy stops declaring what it cannot enforce.
not_enforceable: No hook can force a worktree. A hook observes and refuses; it cannot rewrite a tool call, and it cannot tell from a spawn whether the workers were going to collide.
No hook fires at all when the model decides not to spawn workers, which is the failure this policy is most likely to meet.
Nothing stops a worker inside a worktree from writing an absolute path back into the main checkout. Isolation is a default working directory, not a sandbox.
Nothing merges the branches. If the lead ends the stage without integrating, the work sits on branches under .claude/worktrees/ and the stage looks finished.
This policy is therefore a rule for agents to follow and for reviewers to check, in the same way the file-ownership rule always was. Writing it down is what makes the omission visible.
constraints_from_the_platform: worktree.baseRef in .claude/settings.json decides what a new worktree branches from. The default 'fresh' branches from origin/<default-branch>, so an isolated worker does NOT see the feature branch you are standing on or any unpushed commit. Set it to 'head' for work that continues a branch, or the workers will build against the wrong base and the merge will be enormous.
isolation: "worktree" and cwd are mutually exclusive on a spawn.

EnterWorktree cannot create a worktree from a worker whose working directory was pinned at launch, because that would move the parent session's process-wide directory. Such a worker can only switch into an existing worktree of the same repository by path.
ExitWorktree only touches a worktree that EnterWorktree created in the same session, and refuses to remove one with uncommitted changes unless discard_changes is set.
A worktree that the worker left unchanged is deleted automatically, so an empty result is not evidence the isolation failed.

Background sessions are already isolated by default: worktree.bgIsolation defaults to 'worktree', which blocks Edit and Write in the main checkout until EnterWorktree is called. A background stage that edits without isolating does not corrupt the checkout, it stops.
isolation: "remote" also exists and runs the worker in a remote environment. It is always a background task and its availability is gated, so it is not a general answer to a parallel-edit collision.

decision_rule: Can one role finish this without waiting on anyone? -> inline or subagent.
Do I only need the answer? -> subagent.
Do the workers need to talk to each other to reach the answer? -> team.
Would the workers edit the same files? -> only with isolation 'worktree' and a declared integration step. In a shared checkout, no.
Is the session non-interactive? -> not a team; teammates do not spawn under -p.
Do the workers need to run the build, the test suite or a formatter? -> isolation 'worktree', even if their source files are disjoint: those write shared build output, lockfiles and caches.
constraints_from_the_platform: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default; they require CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1.
Teammates spawn only in interactive sessions.

Teammates cannot spawn teammates, so a team is never nested. A teammate can still spawn ordinary subagents, so depth below a team member follows the platform's subagent nesting limit rather than stopping at one level.
A teammate's model is fixed at spawn time. Permission mode is not: teammates start in the lead's mode and individual modes can be changed after spawning, but cannot be set per teammate at spawn time.
A subagent definition's tools and model apply to a teammate, but its skills and mcpServers do not.
A teammate's idle notification does not carry its output.

With agent teams enabled, any subagent named from the main conversation launches as a teammate, including in stages declared execution: subagent. An idle notification carries no output, so a stage written as spawn-then-wait stalls instead of failing. Enabling teams is therefore a session-level decision, not a per-stage one.
cost_discipline: A stage declaring execution 'team' must say in its actions why parallelism is worth the multiplier.
Disjoint file ownership is stated in the spawn prompt, not assumed. Where it cannot be disjoint, isolation 'worktree' is stated in the spawn instead, and the integration step with it.
The lead coordinates and synthesises; it does not implement while teammates work.
Isolation is not free: a checkout per worker, and a merge the lead must run and test. Count the merge before choosing parallelism, not after the branches exist.

resolution.description: How a task's execution mode is chosen at the moment it runs, rather than inherited from what its stage declared. A stage says what kind of work it is; only the runtime knows whether teams are available, whether siblings would collide, and how much is in flight.
resolution.why: A declared mode is a recommendation made before the situation existed. `execution: team` on a stage is correct advice and wrong instruction in a headless session, where teammates do not spawn at all. Resolving at runtime turns the declaration into a starting point that gets overruled by facts.
inputs: whether agent teams are actually available
whether the role can write at all
whether a sibling holds the same coupled surface
how many tasks are already running

rules.why: Teams are experimental, off by default and interactive-only. Nothing in the lifecycle may depend on them, so an unavailable team degrades rather than failing.
A reviewer that cannot write has nothing to isolate. Giving it a worktree costs setup and disk to protect files it could not have touched.
CRITICAL work is not sent to the background. The point of the risk tier is that somebody is watching, and a background task is precisely the one nobody is.
Two tasks that would edit the same coupled surface are isolated rather than sequenced when both are otherwise ready, so the parallelism survives and the integration becomes an explicit step.
Parallel writers in one checkout produce a build output nobody owns. The cost is real -- setup, disk, a merge -- which is why it applies only when something else is genuinely running.
No fact overruled the stage's recommendation, so it stands.

never.team: in a non-interactive session, or for a task no other task runs alongside
never.background: for CRITICAL risk, or where the next step needs the result
never.worktree: for a role with no write tools

resolution.not_enforceable: Nothing makes an agent honour the resolved mode. A PreToolUse hook can refuse a spawn but cannot rewrite one, so this resolves and records; it does not compel.
